title: Defining Infrastructure
notes:
SCRIPT FOR SLIDE 3: DEFINING INFRASTRUCTURE

There is no single agreed definition of infrastructure, so I start from what the set texts say and then build our own. Three definitions follow, from the broadest to the most finance-oriented.

1. Jochimsen (1966), as quoted in Weber, Staub-Bisang and Alfen (2016), p. 11. Weber et al. present it as one of the broadest definitions on record. The full sentence reads: "the sum of all material, institutional and personal assets, facilities and conditions available to an economy based on the division of labour and its individual economic units that contribute to realising the assimilation of factor remuneration, given an expedient allocation of resources." They add that Jochimsen separates material infrastructure (physical assets, equipment and facilities), institutional infrastructure (the norms and rules a society develops over time) and personal infrastructure (the number and qualities of people). The slide quotes the first clause only.
Reference: Jochimsen, R. (1966) Theorie der Infrastruktur: Grundlagen der marktwirtschaftlichen Entwicklung. Tübingen: J.C.B. Mohr (in German). The wording is Weber et al.'s translation. I have not seen the original.

2. Abor, Macomber, Arun and Murinde (2025), chapter 1, Introduction to the Handbook of Infrastructure Finance, p. 3. The authors write that "there is no universally accepted definition of infrastructure" and that two approaches are common in the literature. The narrow approach "considers infrastructure as physical assets to support economic development". The broader approach is "encompassing not only the physical assets that drive economic development but also the systems and services necessary for supporting broader socio-economic activities". Page 4 adds that on the broader approach infrastructure includes social infrastructure such as schools, universities, hospitals and courts.
Reference: Abor, J.Y., Macomber, J., Arun, T. and Murinde, V. (eds) (2025) The Routledge Handbook of Infrastructure Finance. Routledge.

3. Weber, Staub-Bisang and Alfen (2016), section 1.3, p. 13. After reviewing the competing definitions they say the book addresses material infrastructure, which "includes all physical assets, equipment and facilities of interrelated systems and their necessary service providers offering related commodities and services to the individual economic entities or the wider public with the aim of enabling, sustaining or enhancing societal living conditions". On the same page they build on Fulmer (2009), who proposes "the physical components of interrelated systems providing commodities and services essential to enable, sustain, or enhance societal living conditions".
Reference: Weber, B., Staub-Bisang, M. and Alfen, H.W. (2016) Infrastructure as an Asset Class: Investment Strategy, Sustainability, Project Finance and PPP. 2nd edn. Wiley.

The page numbers are the printed page numbers of each book. Those for Weber et al. come from the PDF and those for Abor et al. from the print-page markers in the EPUB. Check them against the library copies before publishing the script to students.

What the three share. Each includes physical or material assets, and each ties them to what the economy and society need from them: an economy and its economic units (Jochimsen), economic development and socio-economic activities (Abor et al.), and the economic entities or the wider public and societal living conditions (Weber et al.). Abor et al. and Weber et al. also bring in the systems and services around the assets. Only Jochimsen puts institutions and people inside the definition.

Our working definition. Infrastructure is the set of physical assets, together with the systems and services that operate them, that enable economic activity and sustain living conditions in a society. It keeps the common core and leaves institutions and people outside the definition, so they appear later in the course as the conditions under which the assets are financed and run.

title: Key Properties of Infrastructure
notes:
Work through the six properties in turn and test each against a specific asset. Very few assets have all six. A merchant power plant has high sunk costs and a long life but no monopoly and highly elastic revenue. A data centre has almost none of them, yet sits in infrastructure funds.

On political salience. Infrastructure services are things everyone uses and pays for, such as water bills, tolls, rail fares and power prices, so what they cost and how well they work is easy to see and easy to blame the government for. Governments therefore step in on prices, service standards and investment, and they do so after the investor has committed its capital. The investor cannot move the asset, because of the high sunk cost, so it cannot walk away when the terms change. The result is that the price control, the concession or the contract is never settled for good. It can be reopened when a government changes, when bills rise or when a service fails. This is a risk that sits alongside the natural monopoly point, because regulation exists to replace competition and a regulator answers to politicians. It returns in Week 2 on regulation and renegotiation, and in Week 3 when investors price political and regulatory risk.
text: Key Properties of Infrastructure 4 High sunk cost: capital is committed up front and cannot be redeployed, since a bridge has no alternative use and no resale market. Long asset life: thirty to a hundred years or more, which pushes the valuation weight into distant and poorly observed cash flows. Natural monopoly: minimum efficient scale often exceeds market size, so competition in the market is infeasible and regulation substitutes for it. Inelastic demand: the service is close to essential, so volumes are less sensitive to price and to the economic cycle than for most goods. Externalities: costs and benefits fall on parties outside the transaction, which is the standard justification for public involvement. Political salience: the public sees what infrastructure costs and how well it performs, so governments intervene on prices and standards and the terms agreed with an investor can be reopened.

title: A Changing Landscape
notes:
The table scores six assets that investors hold as infrastructure against the six properties on the previous slide. Each one pushes the boundary in a different way. The data centre has capital intensity and a contracted tenant but no monopoly and a short technology life. The tower has a long-lived structure and a short technology cycle. Care homes and student housing are social infrastructure in form and real estate in economics, with demand risk on the operator. Fibre has real network economics, but overbuild has eroded the monopoly. Renewable generation looks like infrastructure while the contract runs and becomes a commodity price bet when it ends. Rolling stock and aircraft are mobile assets with a resale market, which is closer to leasing.

The slide works as a small-group exercise. Give each group two assets and have them argue for and against inclusion using the six properties. The disagreement is the lesson.

Why the boundary problem matters, and why this slide is titled A Changing Landscape. If the category expands to include whatever can be sold as infrastructure, then the empirical claims made about the category stop being reliable. Historical return series, correlation estimates and default statistics are all computed on a definition that has moved.

When an investor reports that infrastructure has delivered stable, inflation-linked returns with low correlation to equities, the first question is which assets were in the sample and whether they resemble what is being bought today. We return to this in Block D and again in Week 6. This is the intellectual thread that connects Week 1 to Week 6, so flag it explicitly and students will hear the callback later.

title: Main Sectors
notes:
The table sets the five main sectors against six dimensions. The colour marks how challenging each dimension is for an investor: red is the most challenging, amber moderate and green the least. The ratings are judgements for discussion, and they rest on the following.

Transport. Demand risk is severe and forecastable only within wide bounds, and network effects mean the value of a link depends on links the owner does not control.
Energy. The sector splits sharply between regulated networks, which are the archetype of infrastructure, and generation, which is increasingly a commodity business. The amber cells reflect that split.
Water and waste. This is the strongest natural monopoly case, with the heaviest regulation and the most politically exposed pricing. Demand is close to essential and stable, so the challenge sits in regulation and politics.
Digital. Technology changes fast against long asset lives, and it is the newest entrant to the category and the least tested.
Social. There is no user revenue, so the covenant of the paying authority is the whole credit, and political risk is the dominant risk.

The cells not stated in those descriptions, such as the technology rating for transport and the track record for water, are my judgement and should be checked before the slide is used. Say this line aloud and keep it off the slide: what they share is a contractual or regulatory structure that converts an asset into a revenue stream. It is the analytical move the block has made since the definition.

title: A Few Useful Taxonomies
notes:
These are the three ways investors cut the market, and together they give the texture of what is on offer.

Economic and social infrastructure. The distinction matters because it determines who bears demand risk. In economic infrastructure the asset owner is often exposed to how many people use the asset. In social infrastructure the state pays for availability whether or not the building is busy. That one difference explains much of the risk profile discussed in Week 4. Sources: Weber, Staub-Bisang and Alfen (2016), section 1.3; Abor et al. (2025), chapter 3.

Regulated, contracted or merchant. Practitioners classify by revenue model rather than by sector, because the revenue model determines the risk. Two toll roads in the same country can sit in different categories if one has an availability payment and the other does not. This is the single most useful classification in the block. Sources: Weber et al. (2016), chapter 3; Gatti (2024), section 1.3.4.

Greenfield and brownfield. Greenfield assets carry construction, completion and commissioning risk, have no operating history to underwrite against, and offer a higher expected return with a wider distribution of outcomes, which is where the cost overrun evidence in Block F bites hardest. Brownfield assets are operating, so construction risk is behind them and operating and regulatory risk remain, with a lower expected return and a narrower distribution. Most institutional capital goes to brownfield even though the investment need is for new assets. The capital wants a risk profile that the need does not offer, and Week 3 returns to this as the central puzzle of private participation.

title: The Ownership and Control Spectrum
notes:
This spectrum recurs in Week 4 as the comparative review of procurement routes. Introduce it here so students have a map before they meet the contractual detail. The two variables that do the work are ownership and demand risk, and they do not move together.

Each row has two examples chosen from different regions or different sectors, so that students see that the arrangement and the sector are separate choices. Statistics on the slide are listed with their sources below. "Checked" means I opened the source in October 2026 and the figure is as stated. "Secondary" means the figure comes from a news report, a reference site or a search summary of the primary page, and should be confirmed at source before the slide is used with students. Descriptions that carry no figure are background and have not been checked against a source.

PUBLIC PROVISION

1. US Interstate Highway System (roads, United States). The Interstate System is the national network of limited-access motorways, built by state highway departments with federal funding and authorised by Congress in 1956. It carries no tolls on most of its length, and the states own and maintain it, so the state bears the demand risk. Slide statistic: about 48,600 miles in 2022. Source, checked: Federal Highway Administration, Highway Statistics 2022, Table HM-20, https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics/2022/hm20.cfm. The US total in the table is 29,382 miles of rural Interstate and 19,223 miles of urban Interstate, which adds to 48,605 miles. Other sources give between 46,000 and 49,000 miles depending on the year and on whether overlapping routes are counted.

2. Thames Barrier (flood defence, England). The barrier is a set of ten steel gates across the River Thames near Woolwich that close to protect central London from tidal surges and storms from the North Sea. It became operational in 1982 and is run and maintained by the Environment Agency, a public body, as part of London's flood defences. It earns no revenue, so it is a clear case of the state providing an asset that generates a public benefit and no user charge. It had been closed 221 times for flood defence by 17 November 2025. Slide statistics: 520 metres, ten gates, 125 square kilometres of central London protected. Source, checked: GOV.UK, The Thames Barrier, https://www.gov.uk/guidance/the-thames-barrier.

PUBLIC CORPORATION

3. Panama Canal (shipping, Panama). The canal is run by the Panama Canal Authority, an autonomous state body that operates it as a commercial business, funded by the tolls it charges ships, so the corporation bears the demand risk with the state behind it. The Authority reported 13,404 transits in fiscal year 2025, of which 3,342 were Neopanamax and 10,062 were Panamax vessels, and cargo of 489.1 million PC/UMS tons. Revenue was B/.5,705 million and net profit B/.4,134 million. The balboa is at par with the US dollar, so revenue was about US$5.7 billion. These are preliminary, unaudited results released on 8 October 2025. Transits had fallen to 11,240 in the drought year before. Slide statistics: 13,404 transits and about US$5.7 billion of revenue in fiscal year 2025. Source, checked: Panama Canal Authority, https://pancanal.com/en/panama-canal-maintains-operational-and-financial-strength/ (the 2024 transit figure is from a Seatrade Maritime report of the same results, https://www.seatrade-maritime.com/maritime-transportation/panama-canal-transits-in-fy2025-bounce-back-from-drought, secondary).

4. China Telecom's Inner Mongolia Information Park (data centres, China). The park is a data centre campus in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, developed and operated by China Telecom, a state-owned telecommunications group. It is widely listed as the largest data centre in the world by floor area. BlackRidge Research gives 994,062 square metres and an estimated 150 MW, which puts it sixth by capacity, behind the Citadel campus in Nevada and others. The size is disputed. One analysis reported by SlashGear suggests that the built area is about a tenth of the headline figure and that the park is unfinished. Which data centre is the largest depends on whether size means floor area, live power or planned capacity. Slide statistic: about 994,000 square metres. The 150 MW estimate is in the script only. Source, secondary: BlackRidge Research, Top 10 Biggest Data Centers in the World, https://www.blackridgeresearch.com/blog/top-biggest-data-centers-in-the-world-location-capacity; SlashGear, https://www.slashgear.com/2048539/largest-data-center-china-telecom-inner-mongolia-information-park/.

AVAILABILITY PPP

5. Royal Children's Hospital (health, Australia). The new hospital in Parkville, Melbourne, was procured by the state of Victoria under its Partnerships Victoria framework. A project agreement was signed on 20 November 2007 with Children's Health Partnership, a private consortium that finances, designs, builds and maintains the facility. The state keeps responsibility for the clinical services. The hospital has about 96,000 square metres of gross floor area and 50 more beds than the old one. The state pays quarterly service payments over the 25-year operating phase, which the Auditor-General put at A$3.742 billion in nominal terms, or A$1.016 billion in net present value as at 30 June 2008. The winning bid had a net present cost of A$946 million at financial close in December 2007, 6.9 per cent below the public sector comparator, and about A$1.38 billion of debt and equity was contributed at financial close. Slide statistic: A$3.7 billion of state service payments over 25 years. Source, checked: Victorian Auditor-General's Office, The New Royal Children's Hospital: a public private partnership (2009), https://www.audit.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/the-new-royal-children-hospital-full-report.pdf.

6. PortMiami Tunnel (roads, United States). The twin tunnels, each about 3,900 feet long, link the Port of Miami to the highway network and take freight traffic off Miami's downtown streets. It was procured by the Florida Department of Transportation as a design, build, finance and maintain availability payment concession. The state pays the concessionaire for the tunnel being available and meeting performance standards, with deductions if it does not, and no tolls are charged, so the state bears the traffic risk. Availability payments are $32.479 million a year in 2009 dollars, indexed, for 30 years. The state also paid $100 million in milestone payments during construction and a $350 million payment on completion. Total project cost was $1,113 million, funded with $80.3 million of equity from Meridiam (90 per cent) and Bouygues (10 per cent) and a federal TIFIA loan of about $341 million. Construction reached substantial completion on 3 August 2014. Slide statistic: availability payments of about US$32 million a year for 30 years, in 2009 dollars. Source, checked: Federal Highway Administration, Port of Miami Tunnel project profile, https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/ipd/project_profiles/fl_port_miami_tunnel.aspx. Other sources describe the whole concession as 35 years, which includes the construction period.

CONCESSION

7. Highway 407 ETR (roads, Canada). The 407 Express Toll Route is a toll motorway north of Toronto. In April 1999 the Ontario government approved a C$3.1 billion offer from a contractor-led consortium for a 99-year lease of the road, and the lessee sets and collects the tolls, so it bears the traffic risk. The operator's own facts page gives 108 km and reports average weekday trips rising from 237,000 in 1999 to over 413,000 in 2017. Slide statistics: 108 km, and a 99-year lease sold in 1999 for about C$3.1 billion. Sources: the lease price is checked against the Transportation Research Board record, https://trid.trb.org/View/503863. The 108 km figure and the trip figures are secondary: they come from the operator's facts page at https://www.407etr.com/en/highway/corporate/background-information2.html as reported in a search summary, because the page could not be read directly. Confirm them there.

8. Manila Water (water, Philippines). Manila Water holds the concession to supply water and wastewater services to the East Zone of Metro Manila. The concession agreement with the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System was signed in August 1997 for 25 years. A 15-year extension in 2009 moved the end date from 2022 to 2037. The company serves over six million people in 23 cities and municipalities, and water availability rose from 26 per cent in 1997 to 99 per cent. Customers pay tariffs set under the concession's regulatory rules, so the concessionaire bears the demand risk. Slide statistics: a 1997 concession extended to 2037, serving over six million people. Sources, secondary: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Water, and company information reported in a search summary. One version of the Wikipedia history says the extension ran until 2024. The company's own filings and press reports say 2037, so the 2037 date is used. Confirm in the company's annual report.

REGULATED PRIVATE

9. Thames Water (water, England). Thames Water supplies water and wastewater services to about 16 million customers in London and the south east of England. It is privately owned and regulated by Ofwat through five-year price controls, which set what it may charge on its regulatory asset base. In its annual results for the year to 31 March 2026, released on 15 July 2026, net debt on a statutory basis rose to £18,516 million, gearing was 86 per cent, and the regulatory capital value was £22,725 million. Capital investment was a record £2,680 million. Debt is therefore close to the regulated asset base, which is why the company's finances sit at the centre of the debate on financialisation in Week 3. The company was seeking a creditor-led rescue and its position may have changed. Slide statistics: net debt of £18.5 billion against a regulatory capital value of £22.7 billion in March 2026. Source, checked: Thames Water, Annual Results for the year to 31 March 2026, https://www.thameswater.co.uk/news/2026/jul/thames-water-annual-results-2025-26. The customer figure is from a press description and is not on the slide.

10. Heathrow Airport (aviation, England). Heathrow is the UK's hub airport. It is privately owned and its charges to airlines are set under a price control by the Civil Aviation Authority, so its return depends on a regulatory settlement that is separate from its planning consents. It handled about 84.5 million passengers in 2025, up 0.7 per cent on 83.9 million in 2024, with 1 August the busiest day at about 270,000 passengers. Slide statistic: 84.5 million passengers in 2025. Source, secondary: Centre for Aviation, 12 January 2026, https://centreforaviation.com/news/london-heathrow-airport-handles-record-pax-in-dec-2025-and-full-year-2025-1344700, and Business Travel News Europe, https://www.businesstravelnewseurope.com/Air-Travel/London-Heathrow-sets-passenger-record-of-84-5-million-for-2025. One outlet gives 84.4 million. Confirm against Heathrow's own release before use. The Week 2 deck covers the consenting and regulatory setting in more detail.

FULL PRIVATE

11. Switch's Citadel campus (data centres, United States). The Citadel campus is a privately owned data centre campus at the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center in Nevada. Switch's own site describes a campus of over 2,000 acres projected to reach over 12 million square feet of data centre space and up to 2 GW at full completion. Older rankings credit the campus with 650 MW and about 669,000 square metres and call it the largest operating data centre campus. Other sources give different targets, such as 7.2 million square feet in older reports and 17.4 million square feet and 850 MW on a data centre listing site. The owner bears the demand risk, which it covers by letting space to tenants. Slide statistics: 12 million square feet and up to 2 GW, both planned. Source, checked: Switch, https://www.switch.com/?p=32392. Ranking, secondary: BlackRidge Research, as above.

12. ERCOT merchant generators (power, Texas). Most of Texas is served by a grid operated by the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which runs an energy-only wholesale market in which generators earn the market price and are not paid separately for capacity. Generators there are the standard example of merchant exposure, with revenue that moves with wholesale prices and the economic cycle. ERCOT's all-time peak demand record is 85,508 MW, set on 10 August 2023, and it is unofficial until final settlements. Slide statistic: record peak demand of 85,508 MW in 2023 (10 August). Source, secondary: ERCOT, Yearly Peak Demand Records, https://www.ercot.com/static-assets/data/news/content/a-peak-demand/all-time-records.htm, read through a search result because the page blocks automated access. The description of the energy-only market is background and has not been checked here.

title: Infrastructure and Economic Development
notes:
OUTLINE OF BLOCK B, AND WHY THE CLAIM IS HARD TO TEST

Every infrastructure prospectus, ministerial speech and multilateral report opens with the same claim, that infrastructure investment raises output. The claim is plausible, widely believed and hard to establish. If students take one methodological point from Week 1, it should be this one, and it returns in Week 6 when we ask whether the returns attributed to infrastructure are returns to infrastructure.

Rich countries have more infrastructure and also more of everything else, and governments build where growth is already expected. A correlation between infrastructure stock and output tells us almost nothing on its own. The difficulty is identification and not measurement. Three problems recur. Reverse causality: output growth generates the tax revenue and the demand that produce infrastructure, so the arrow can run either way. Omitted variables: institutional quality, human capital and openness all move with both infrastructure and output. Heterogeneity: the effect of a road in a congested corridor and a road in an empty one are not the same number, so a single pooled coefficient may describe neither. Each has a standard remedy, and none is fully convincing on its own. The literature has converged on panel methods with instrument or dynamic-panel identification, and on being honest about what remains.

The block runs through three papers that give very different answers. Each has two slides, one of background and one showing the main output of an interactive page in Lecture Notes/Week 1/web/ (the button at the top right of the second slide opens it). A final slide summarises.

title: Aschauer (1989): The Case for a Large Effect
notes:
SOURCE AND VERIFICATION

Aschauer, D. A. (1989), Is public expenditure productive?, Journal of Monetary Economics 23(2), 177 to 200. The article is not open access and I could not obtain the full text, so no table or figure from it is reproduced. What the slide states rests on these secondary sources.
The elasticity of 0.39: Mas and Maudos (2004), who report that Aschauer's Cobb-Douglas estimate gave an elasticity of 0.39 for national public infrastructure (https://www.uv.es/maudosj/publicaciones/mas%20y%20maudos%202004.pdf).
The 1949 to 1985 annual sample, the core infrastructure finding and the weak role of military capital: the abstract as recorded in TRID (https://trid.trb.org/View/300513) and a second reference noting annual data for 1949 to 1985.
The criticism, and later estimates ranging from negative values to well above the return to private capital: Aschauer (1997), Levy Institute Working Paper 189 (https://levyinstitute.org/pubs/wp189.pdf), as reported in a search summary.
If the paper's own table is wanted on the slide, supply the PDF and it can be reproduced.

TEACHING POINT

Aschauer's finding launched the modern literature and was almost immediately doubted. An elasticity of 0.39 is difficult to reconcile with any equilibrium account of investment. The subsequent thirty years have been an extended argument about identification, and the estimates have fallen steadily as the identification has improved. Calderón and colleagues arrive at roughly a quarter of Aschauer's figure. The trajectory is itself the lesson: early estimates of the returns to a fashionable investment class are usually too high, and the correction comes from better identification and not from new data. The parallel with the infrastructure return literature in Block D is exact.

title: Ansar et al. (2016): Evidence from 95 Chinese Projects
notes:
FIGURE REPRODUCED

Figure 6 of Ansar, A., Flyvbjerg, B., Budzier, A. and Lunn, D. (2016), Does infrastructure investment lead to economic growth or economic fragility? Evidence from China, Oxford Review of Economic Policy 32(3), 360 to 390, page 377. The article is open access (DOI 10.1093/oxrep/grw022) and the copy used is in Resources/Week 1/Infrastructure and Economic Development/. The horizontal axis is cost overrun (actual over estimated cost) and the vertical axis is benefit shortfall (actual over estimated benefits), so a project's ex post ratio is its appraisal ratio multiplied by the vertical value and divided by the horizontal one. The authors estimate the ratios from cost and traffic volumes and do not measure them directly.

THE DATA

The projects were drawn from the loan documents of the Asian Development Bank and the World Bank. All transport projects for which valid and reliable cost and schedule data could be found are included, which is why the authors call the dataset the largest of its kind on China. Table 3: the average cost overrun was 27.5 per cent for roads (74 projects), 41.5 per cent for rail (21 projects) and 30.6 per cent in total, with a standard deviation of 46.9; the median was 18.5 per cent, and 70 per cent of roads and 90 per cent of rail projects went over budget (page 373). The comparison with 806 projects in rich democracies uses a Wilcoxon test (W = 38712, p = 0.8591) and finds no significant difference; the authors treat that as preliminary because they could not control for project size or start year (page 372). Traffic data cover 156 projects (137 roads and 19 rail). The average shortfall of only 5.0 per cent hides two extremes: 64.7 per cent of projects fell short by 41.2 per cent on average and 35.3 per cent exceeded forecast by 61.4 per cent, which caused congestion (pages 374 and 375, Figure 5). Planners expected a benefit-cost ratio of 1.4 to 1.5.

THE CLAIM AND ITS LIMITS

The authors' hypothesis is that, owing to a propensity to cost overruns and benefit shortfalls, the typical infrastructure investment destroys economic value, and their policy proposition is that less is more. Only six of 66 projects were outright successes. Be fair to both sides. Calderón and Ansar do not measure the same object: one is an aggregate production function and the other is the project-level ex post performance of one country's transport projects. The projects are those with IFI documentation, so they may not be representative, and the paper is contested.

Simulated, 54 per cent of projects fall below 1.0, 17 per cent lie between 1.0 and 1.45, and 28 per cent are above. The paper reports 55, 17 and 28 per cent for 65 projects (with its middle band running from 1.0 to 1.4). The match to within a point supports using the published moments as a summary of the data, although the independence assumption is untested.

THE RIGHT PANEL

A portfolio of five projects can show anything from none paying to all of them paying. A portfolio of 95 pays in about 46 per cent of projects, give or take about five points. This is the same lesson as the country sampling page: one project, like one country, is a poor guide to the pattern, and a pool is a good one.

The interactive page also reports the appraisal ratio at which the median project would break even once the paper's average pattern of overruns and shortfalls is applied, about 1.56. That is a reference class adjustment, of the kind Week 6 uses and a group project can apply to a real base case.

title: Summary
notes:
CLOSE THE BLOCK ON THE LAST ITEM

The three papers do not disagree. An elasticity is an average over projects that were built. It contains the successful bypass and the airport with no passengers, and it cannot separate them. For a country with a thin network the marginal project may beat the average, and for one that has built the obvious things it will fall below it. Selection, not volume, is where the returns are made or lost. A national target expressed in pounds or per cent of GDP is an input measure, and inputs are not outcomes. Make students do the arithmetic aloud: ten per cent more infrastructure for one per cent more output changes how they read a ministerial announcement.

NEWER EVIDENCE (verified at abstract level)

I checked the bibliographic details and headline findings below against abstracts, working papers and policy briefs found by search in October 2026, not against the full texts. Check any number before quoting it.
Donaldson, D. (2018), Railroads of the Raj: estimating the impact of transportation infrastructure, American Economic Review 108(4-5), 899 to 934: railroads decreased trade costs, increased trade and raised real income levels in colonial India. Similar in spirit to a positive elasticity, and identified from a trade model and from lines approved but never built.
Asher, S. and Novosad, P. (2020), Rural roads and local economic development, American Economic Review 110(3), 797 to 823: India's rural road programme, identified from a population threshold, left agricultural investment, production and household consumption unchanged, and workers moved out of farming. Different from the positive aggregate estimates.
Faber, B. (2014), Trade integration, market size and industrialization: evidence from China's National Trunk Highway System, Review of Economic Studies 81(3), 1046 to 1070: connection to the highway network reduced GDP growth in non-targeted peripheral counties, through lower industrial output growth. The distributional point on the old Block B slide, and consistent with Ansar's doubts about China.
Allen, T. and Arkolakis, C. (2022), The welfare effects of transportation infrastructure improvements, Review of Economic Studies 89(6), 2911 to 2957: in a spatial equilibrium model with congestion applied to the United States highway network, returns are on average positive but highly variable, which shows the importance of well-targeted investment. The closest to our summary.
Burlig, F. and Preonas, L. (2024), Out of the darkness and into the light? Development effects of rural electrification, Journal of Political Economy 132(9), 2937 to 2971: India's rural electrification programme expanded access substantially but had limited economic impacts after three to five years.
Donaldson, D. and Hornbeck, R. (2016), Railroads and American economic growth: a market access approach, Quarterly Journal of Economics 131(2), 799 to 858: changes in market access from railroads were capitalised into agricultural land values, and removing the railroads would have cost a large share of their value (the percentages differ across drafts, so do not quote one without checking the article).
Jedwab, R. and Storeygard, A. (2022), The average and heterogeneous effects of transportation investments: evidence from sub-Saharan Africa 1960 to 2010, Journal of the European Economic Association 20(1), 1 to 38: positive average effects of market access on city population, larger for small and remote cities.
For Block D (finance): Andonov, A., Kräussl, R. and Rauh, J. (2021), Institutional investors and infrastructure investing, Review of Financial Studies 34(8), 3880 to 3934: infrastructure funds show weak risk-adjusted performance and cash flows as volatile and cyclical as private equity, yet attract growing commitments from public investors.

RESERVE MATERIAL FROM THE EARLIER BLOCK B SLIDES

Comparison of the three papers. Aschauer (1989): United States annual data 1949 to 1985, production function in levels, elasticity 0.39, cannot rule out spurious correlation between trending series or reverse causation. Calderón et al. (2015): 88 countries 1960 to 2000, pooled mean group estimator with one long-run slope, elasticity 0.07 to 0.10, cannot show which projects were built. Ansar et al. (2016): 95 road and rail projects in China 1984 to 2008 and 806 in rich democracies, ex post cost and traffic against appraisal, 55 per cent below a ratio of 1, cannot show network effects or benefits other than traffic.
Channels through which infrastructure affects output: direct productivity (infrastructure as an input), market access, agglomeration (density raises productivity through matching, sharing and learning), human capital (water, sanitation, electricity and digital access, with long lags) and crowding in. The channels operate over very different horizons, which is one reason short-run evaluations of infrastructure programmes tend to disappoint. The agglomeration channel is the one land economy students will know from urban economics, so use it as the anchor.
Distribution: an elasticity is silent about who gains, and a link that raises national output can concentrate activity in the larger of two places. Appraisal in the United Kingdom has argued for a decade about place-weighted benefit-cost ratios. Agglomeration: the wider economic impact of higher effective density is counted as an additional benefit in United Kingdom transport appraisal, and the elasticity applied to density can decide whether a scheme passes. I removed two claims from the earlier draft that I could not verify (that wider economic impact is the largest single benefit in most United Kingdom appraisals, and that six of the seventeen Sustainable Development Goals depend directly on infrastructure); check the Department for Transport's TAG guidance and Abor et al. (2025) chapters 3 and 16 before restoring any figure. Access: access asks who is connected where growth asks what is produced, and development finance institutions are mandated on access rather than return.

SEMINAR TASKS

1. Reconcile an output elasticity of about 0.08 with the finding that the typical project destroys value, and state what would have to be true for both to hold. A good answer says that the two numbers measure different things, an average over built projects and the outcome of individual projects, and that a positive stock elasticity is compatible with negative marginal returns when selection is poor. It can use the interactive pages: the pooled elasticity is stable across samples of countries while the share of projects that pay is stable across portfolios at about 46 per cent.
2. Set out the institutional arrangements you would require before approving a national investment programme, given that selection matters more than volume.
3. Identify the conditions under which a new transport link makes the smaller of the two places it connects worse off.

title: Ambition and Efficiency Drive the Estimate
notes:
FIGURE AND SOURCE

The chart is redrawn from Figure O.1 of Rozenberg and Fay (eds) (2019), Beyond the Gap, Overview, page 6, and the sector values are those printed in the figure, in US$ billion a year for low- and middle-income countries, 2015 to 2030. Electricity: 298, 778, 1,020. Transport: 157, 417, 1,060. Water supply and sanitation: 116, 198, 229. Flood protection: 23, 103, 335. Irrigation: 43, 50, 100. The sector values add to 637, 1,546 and 2,744, against printed totals of US$640 billion, US$1.5 trillion and US$2.7 trillion, so the printed totals are rounded. The figure itself is a dense rotated table and does not stay legible on a slide, which is why it is redrawn; the original is on PDF page 28 of the Overview. The report is licensed CC BY 3.0 IGO, and the source line credits it. The redrawing is mine.

HOW TO READ IT

The three scenarios are defined in the figure. Minimum: less ambitious goals and high efficiency, which means for example providing only basic water and sanitation and keeping coastal flood risk constant in relative terms. Preferred: ambitious goals and high efficiency, for example safe water and sanitation, Dutch standards of coastal flood protection for cities, and investment in renewable energy now. Maximum: ambitious goals and low efficiency, for example letting cities sprawl, building rail without policies to raise its use, and early-scrapping fossil capacity that was built to give high electricity access quickly. Because only one of the two dimensions changes between neighbouring scenarios, the first step isolates ambition (2.0 to 4.5 per cent of GDP) and the second isolates efficiency (4.5 to 8.2 per cent). The efficiency step also bundles policy choices such as sprawl, so it is not a pure procurement effect, and it should be taught as the cost of an incoherent policy mix as much as of poor delivery.

The report says that for every sector the two most important determinants of cost are the ambition of the goal in access and quality and spending efficiency, which depends on complementary policies and on measures to reduce unit costs such as better procurement, planning or execution (page 5). It says costs for these sectors vary by a factor of 1 to 4, or 2 to 8 per cent of GDP, and that the range does not narrow when only plans compatible with a 2 degree path are considered (pages 4 and 5). It also identifies policy mixes that reach the infrastructure-related SDGs while limiting spending on new infrastructure to 4.5 per cent of GDP a year (page 5), which is the preferred scenario.

THE BENCHMARK METHOD

The report calls the most common method, cross-country benchmarking, not the most useful (page 3). It takes the average stock of infrastructure that countries typically have at different levels of income, urbanisation and economic structure and projects the cost of maintaining that relationship. The report gives two limitations (page 4): there is no assumption of optimality, so if infrastructure was under- or oversupplied in the past the gap will remain, and the estimates are highly sensitive to projected growth and socioeconomic change, with the sensitivity seldom explored. Its alternative is to price explicit goals with costing models and to present results in an if-then form, which is what the chart shows. It also says that it is not possible to determine an optimal level of infrastructure and that planning and investment are inherently a political choice (page 3); this is the link to Week 2.

TEACHING POINT

A gap number is the cost of a chosen goal at an assumed efficiency. The same sectors, countries and years give 2.0 or 8.2 per cent of GDP depending on two assumptions, and the report's contribution is to make the assumptions visible. Link back to Block B: the report notes that infrastructure networks have threshold effects and that the United States interstate system is believed to have had very large impacts until its completion and limited effects afterwards (page 3).

(2021), The Global Infrastructure Gap: Potential, Perils, and a Framework for Distinction, Hoover Institution Working Paper 22009 (Long-Run Prosperity series), March 2021, 68 pages. A copy is in Resources/Week 1/Investment Need and Gap Narrative/. A search shows the paper listed as forthcoming in the Journal of Economic Literature (an AEA conference listing of 2023 and the author's page), but I could not confirm a published issue, so the slide cites the working paper. Check the Journal of Economic Literature site before the reference is changed. Page numbers below are the printed pages of the working paper, which is the PDF page less 2.

THE CHART

The counts are from Table 1 and the text. Paved roads: 21 of 26 poor countries sort into Quadrant I, the quadrant in which the return clears both hurdles (page 14). Electricity: 18 of 49 (page 14), and 15 of those 18 are low-income. Aggregated, 39 of the 75 country and infrastructure observations (52 per cent) clear both hurdles, and those 39 fall across 32 countries, so 21 of the 53 poor countries cleared neither hurdle for either type of infrastructure, that is 40 per cent with no returns-based case for investment (page 19). Of the 32 that did clear, only 7 did so for both roads and electricity (pages 19 and 20), and the middle category of 25 on the chart is the difference (32 less 7). The abstract states the 7 of 53 result and the introduction (page 6) puts it as less than one in seven countries.

THE TEST

The framework is an equilibrium one. Additional investment in a poor country's infrastructure is efficient and can be financed from rich-country private savings if and only if the social return on that infrastructure exceeds both the return on private capital in the poor country and the return on private capital in the rich country (abstract). The authors say the global infrastructure gap closely resembles the financing gap of the Harrod-Domar model: a target level of investment is set, and the gap is the difference between that target and national savings or scheduled investment (page 2). Among the rich countries in the sample, all but Japan sorted into Quadrant III for roads, which means a further dollar earned more in private capital than in roads (page 14).

THE LIMITS

The returns are from Canning, D. and Bennathan, E. (2000), and the cost of building roads and electricity comes from 1985 World Bank data, so in effect the return estimates do too (pages 12 and 13). The authors say that too much has happened since 1985 to draw present-day conclusions from the results (pages 6 and 7), and that the paper offers a template for use with updated data. Their policy conclusion is that the World Bank should update and validate the social-return data before pressing a billions-to-trillions agenda. A discussant at the November 2022 Hoover conference (Ramey, from search results) made the same point about thin current data on returns. Be fair to the paper: it does not say that investment in poor countries is unattractive, and where the hurdles are cleared it reports excess returns that are large (as much as 10.2 times the return on rich-country private capital, page 6, and about seven times the excess return on emerging-market equities before liberalisation).

TEACHING POINT

A gap measures need, and capital follows return. The two can diverge for good reasons, which is why a large gap is evidence of a large obstacle at least as often as of a large opportunity. This is the hinge to Week 3, where the obstacles are currency mismatch, political and regulatory risk and the structure of the investor base, and to Week 4, where bankability and risk allocation turn an investment need into a financeable project.

ECONOMIST READINGS ON THE CLAIM
The claim in the first item has a long press history. The Economist of 22 March 2014, The trillion-dollar gap, moves from the gap to the statement that the greater opportunity lies in private capital, and cites US$50 trillion held by institutional investors, of which 0.8 per cent was in infrastructure (the 2014 figure, not a current one). The Economist of 23 July 2026, The return of the African megaproject, repeats the step twelve years later: with aid cuts and debt service squeezing governments, it says private capital is required to fill the gap, while its own figures show private finance raised in Africa across all industries at US$20.4 billion in 2024. The 2026 line is quoted on the slide under the chart. Setting the two articles side by side shows an inference that has not changed, and Gardner and Henry argue that the returns data needed to test it are out of date. Both articles are journalism reporting other bodies' figures, so name the primary source (World Economic Forum, OECD) and check it before quoting. See Resources/00 Economist readings - what to use where.md.

Block C
The investment need and the gap narrative
Where the trillion-dollar numbers come from, and what they can and cannot support.
Indicative length 30 minutes

---

Every report opens with a gap
The infrastructure investment gap is the most quoted number in the sector and the least interrogated. It appears in multilateral reports, fund marketing and government strategies, usually to two significant figures and usually without a method.

A gap estimate is not an observation. It is the difference between two constructed quantities: what would be spent on current trends, and what should be spent to meet a stated objective. Both halves are modelled, and the second depends entirely on the objective chosen.

---

How a gap estimate is built
Choose an objective. Meeting projected demand, matching a peer group ratio of investment to GDP, or achieving a development goal each produce different answers.
Model required investment. Usually a demand projection converted into physical capacity and then into cost, with unit costs taken from historical averages.
Model trend investment. Extrapolate current spending, which is itself poorly measured in most countries.
Take the difference and aggregate to 2030 or 2040. Small differences in assumed growth compound into trillions over a twenty-year horizon.
Nothing in this procedure establishes that the investment would be worthwhile, only that it would be needed to hit the chosen target.

---

The most quoted figure
US$15tn
Estimated shortfall between projected and required global infrastructure investment to 2040, on the Global Infrastructure Hub Outlook.
The Outlook models required investment at roughly ninety-four trillion dollars to 2040 across transport, energy, water and telecommunications, against projected investment on current trends of about seventy-nine trillion.

The modelled requirement is benchmarked on the performance of best-performing peer countries. Change the peer benchmark and the gap changes by trillions. Add the Sustainable Development Goals for water and electricity access and it grows again.

The figure is useful as an order of magnitude and misleading as a target.
Global Infrastructure Hub, Global Infrastructure Outlook. Figures to be verified against the current edition before delivery.

---

What the gap narrative is used for
Legitimate uses
Establishing an order of magnitude for policy discussion
Comparing relative need across regions and sectors
Identifying which sectors are furthest from a service standard
Making the case that public balance sheets alone will not cover it
Uses that do not follow
Inferring that private capital will earn a return by filling the gap
Treating the gap as a pipeline of investable projects
Reading a large gap as evidence of a large opportunity rather than of a large obstacle
Using it to justify a specific project, which requires appraisal not aggregation

---

Why the gap persists where the need is greatest
If the need is largest in low and middle income countries, and capital is globally mobile, the gap should close. It does not. The obstacles are not a shortage of capital but the terms on which capital will travel: currency mismatch between local revenues and hard currency finance, political and regulatory risk, the absence of a bankable project pipeline, and the sovereign credit ceiling that caps what any project in the jurisdiction can be rated.

These are the subject of Week 3 and Week 4. Introduce them here so that the gap looks like a structural problem rather than a marketing opportunity.
Abor and others (2025), ch. 3; Hainz and Kleimeier (2012).

---

Need is not evenly distributed
Sub-Saharan Africa
The largest gap relative to output, concentrated in electricity access, water and sanitation, and the road network. Also the thinnest domestic capital market.
Asia
The largest gap in absolute terms, driven by urbanisation and by power demand. Considerable domestic savings, unevenly intermediated.
Latin America
A long history of concession-based delivery and an equally long history of renegotiation, which is the Week 2 evidence base.
MENA
Capital is not the constraint. Institutional quality, regulatory predictability and the diversification agenda are.
Europe
Renewal rather than expansion, plus the investment implied by the energy transition. A maintenance problem misdescribed as a growth problem.
North America
An ageing stock, a well-documented maintenance backlog, and a municipal bond market that finances it in a way no other region replicates.
Abor ch. 4 to ch. 9.

---

Public balance sheets and what constrains them
The standard argument for private participation is that governments cannot afford the investment. Stated that way the argument is weak, because a government that can borrow at the sovereign rate can almost always finance an asset more cheaply than a private consortium can.

The stronger arguments are about capability and incentive rather than money: whether the state can manage delivery, whether transferring construction risk to a party that can price it improves outcomes, and whether an off-balance-sheet structure is being used to evade a fiscal rule rather than to improve delivery. Engel, Fischer and Galetovic in Week 2 make this precise.
Engel, Fischer and Galetovic (2013).

---

Block C discussion
Seminar questions
You are asked to produce an infrastructure gap estimate for a single country. What is the first decision you have to make, and how much does the answer depend on it?
A minister cites the global gap figure to justify a specific rail scheme. What is wrong with the inference?
If capital is mobile and the need is greatest in developing economies, why does the capital not go there?

title: Infrastructure as an Asset Class
notes:
OUTLINE OF THE SECTION (ABOUT 20 MINUTES, SIX SLIDES)

The section tests infrastructure's claim to be an asset class, using one regulated utility as the worked case and the academic evidence on the funds that hold such assets. The Economist readings in Resources/Week 1/Infrastructure as an Asset Class/ supply the narrative of the case, and the report and filings supply the figures. Slides 2 to 4 follow Thames Water: its capital structure, the gap between allowed and realised returns, and inflation linkage. Slide 5 turns to the funds. The summary says what survives and where each thread returns.

THE TEST (carried over from the earlier draft; the citation is Weber ch. 2.1 and has not been rechecked)

An asset class is not a marketing category. It is a group of investments whose returns are driven by a common set of economic factors, which behave similarly under stress, and which are not spanned by existing asset classes already in the portfolio. The last condition is the demanding one. If infrastructure returns can be reproduced by a combination of equities, bonds and real estate, infrastructure is a strategy and not an asset class, and it should be priced and benchmarked accordingly. The spanning test is the rigorous version of the question, and stating it makes the later evidence interpretable and not a list of findings.

THE FIVE CLAIMS

Stable cash flows: essential services with inelastic demand, so revenue is less cyclical than corporate earnings. Inflation linkage: tariffs indexed by regulation or contract, so real returns are protected when inflation rises. Low correlation: returns driven by regulatory and contractual factors and not by equity market sentiment. Long duration: cash flows extending decades, matching the liabilities of pension funds and life insurers. Illiquidity premium: compensation for accepting an asset that cannot be sold quickly, earned by investors who do not need to sell.

Insist on the third item on the slide. Every one of the five claims is really a claim about a contract. If the contract expires, or is rewritten, the claim goes with it. That is why the case is a regulated utility, whose contract is rewritten every five years.

This is the transferable tool of the section. A regulated water network is protected against inflation because a regulatory formula indexes the allowed revenue, not because water is inflation-proof. A contracted solar farm is protected for the life of its power purchase agreement and no longer, and a merchant toll road only to the extent the concession allows tolls to rise and traffic tolerates it. (2021), Institutional Investors and Infrastructure Investing, The Review of Financial Studies 34(8), 3880 to 3934, page 3900: capital calls (panels A and B) and distributions (panels C and D) per year in US$ million on a US$10 million commitment, for infrastructure, buyout, venture capital and real estate funds raised from 2002 to 2018, for the full sample and for a matched subsample. The figure is reproduced unaltered except that the journal header and caption are cropped; the caption is quoted in these notes. The article is open access through City, University of London (DOI 10.1093/rfs/hhab048), and a copy is in Resources/Week 1/Infrastructure as an Asset Class/. Page 3882: the authors test, and through their tests reject, the hypothesis that infrastructure investing through closed private funds on average delivers more stable and diversifying cash flows than other alternative asset classes; instead infrastructure investing as institutions practise it has procyclical cash flows generated largely by quick deal exits. The abstract (page 3880) adds that closed funds attract growing commitments, particularly from public investors, despite weak risk-adjusted performance. How to read the figure: the infrastructure line (black) follows the other private fund lines closely, calling capital in the first three years and distributing it from year 4 to year 12, with a similar lifecycle to buyout and real estate funds. The authors say that infrastructure funds have a similar timeline of capital calls to venture capital funds but more distributions early in the fund life.

Tail risk: Bianchi, R. J., Bornholt, G., Drew, M. E. and Howard, M. F. (2014), Long-term US infrastructure returns and portfolio selection, Journal of Banking and Finance 42, 314 to 325. I have checked the abstract and not the full text: they reconstruct United States listed infrastructure index returns from 1927 to 2010 using systematic and industry risk factors; recent returns may understate the long-run tail risk, which is similar to that of a broad portfolio of United States stocks; and they report benefits of holding public infrastructure for mean-variance and mean-CVaR investors. Their finding on tail risk is the one to stress, with the diversification benefit mentioned alongside it. Some indices examined behave differently from others.

Premium: The Economist, 7 November 2019, What is the illiquidity premium? (Buttonwood, Finance and economics). It shows with a worked example how a premium arises from trading costs, cites Amihud and Mendelson (1986) for the point that long-horizon investors can earn it, and warns that liquidity varies over time and that in crises such as 2008 and 2009 investors discover they are less patient than they thought. It is a primer and not evidence that unlisted infrastructure earns such a premium. The premium is plausible in theory and poorly identified in the data, so do not overclaim in either direction.

The market: The Economist, 18 January 2024, Why BlackRock is betting billions on infrastructure (Schumpeter), reports that infrastructure fund assets under management increased almost five-fold over the past decade to US$1.3 trillion according to Preqin, a data provider, and that BlackRock announced on 12 January 2024 that it would buy Global Infrastructure Partners for US$12.5 billion. Preqin is the primary source for the figure and I have not seen it; the deal value is also reported by Reuters.

TEACHING POINT

The asset may be a forty-year asset, and the vehicle is a vehicle of ten years or so. Investors are exposed to the vehicle. This is the single most important empirical finding in the section, and it recurs in Week 3 and Week 5: the distinction between the asset and the wrapper is a theme of the module. The typical contractual life of ten years is stated in the earlier draft and is not verified here. For Week 6, appraisal-based valuations of unlisted funds smooth reported returns and understate volatility and correlation with equities, and a closed-end fund draws capital and pays fees before any asset has been improved or sold, so its reported returns are negative in the early years by construction (the J-curve). Performance of funds against public markets has to be compared with a public market equivalent and not with an internal rate of return alone.

notes:
WHY THIS SLIDE IS HERE

The asset-class section argues that infrastructure's long lives and contracted cash flows give it a distinctive risk, and that the vehicle often differs from the asset. A data centre campus is a clean test, because it combines long-lived structures with equipment that may be obsolete within a few years, and because the funding has moved into new vehicles. The aspect for Week 1 is the cost and life of the asset. Week 3 takes how it is financed.

THE FIGURES

Left panel, from NBER Working Paper 35865 (Van Nieuwerburgh 2026), printed pages 2 and 4: about $11 million a megawatt for the real estate asset including specialised cooling and backup power, $2 million a megawatt for power infrastructure, and $28 million a megawatt for integrated GPU racks (at $4 million a rack), the external network and shared storage, in total about $41 million a megawatt in 2025. A representative 200 MW campus therefore costs about $8.2 billion, of which about two thirds is IT equipment and one third the facility and its power. A campus drawing 200 MW supports about 166.7 MW of critical IT load at a power usage effectiveness of 1.2, which is about 1,170 high-density racks of 142 kW each, and it uses as much electricity in a year as about 170,000 average US households (page 4). Rack density has risen from 5 to 10 kW to well over 100 kW (page 3).

Right panel, page 6 and Figure 1: the combined capital expenditure of Oracle, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet rose from about $97 billion in 2020 to more than $400 billion in 2025 and is projected to exceed $800 billion in 2026, when it passes their combined operating cash flow for the first time. The bars for 2025 and 2026 show the lower bound of 'more than' and are not exact. The data are the author's, taken from company reports and projections that I have not rechecked.

THE POINT ABOUT LIVES AND DEBT

Printed page 7 (cited to Moody's Ratings, 2025): collateral such as GPUs differs from conventional real estate or aircraft because its economic life is shorter and rapid technological change creates substantial obsolescence risk, which makes resale value less certain. Page 13 says that large expansions become financially consequential when there is a mismatch between the adoption of a new technology and the maturity of the debt issued to finance it. The paper gives no figures for asset lives, so the slide gives none. If students ask, say that no source I have read states them and that the question is open. A building can last decades, so the long-lived wrapper (a lease of up to twenty years in the paper's main example, treated in Week 3) can sit on an asset whose most valuable component does not.

THE LINK TO THE REST OF THE SECTION

The claims slide said that infrastructure is long-lived and its cash flows predictable. Here two thirds of the cost is short-lived equipment, and the predictability comes from the tenant's credit and not from the asset, which echoes the point on the Thames Water slides that the cash flow is a regulatory construct. The fees in the fee-drag page are also relevant: a vehicle with a ten-year life holding assets that become obsolete in five years will behave differently from a regulated network.

QUESTIONS FOR THE ROOM

If two thirds of the cost has a short life and the debt runs for twenty years, who holds the residual value risk? Is a data centre campus infrastructure in the sense of the Week 1 definition, or a property with an equipment lease? Which of the five properties on the key properties slide does it fail?

title: Summary
notes:
CLOSE THE SECTION ON THE FIRST TWO ITEMS

The strong version of the asset class claim does not survive the tests. A weaker version does, and it is the version worth teaching: certain infrastructure assets, held directly, with a regulated or contracted revenue base and a long holding period, provide long-duration, partially indexed cash flow that is difficult to obtain elsewhere. The qualifications are doing real work in that sentence. If time is short, end the section here.

WHERE THE THREADS RETURN

The module timetable (in the original Week 1 deck and the course outline) is: Week 2 institutional frameworks and stakeholder governance; Week 3 private investment in infrastructure; Week 4 infrastructure financing and deal structuring; Week 5 intermediation and deal brokerage; Week 6 performance and valuation; Week 7 sustainability, ESG and emerging trends. Week 2 covers economic regulation and the price control, of which Thames Water is the standing example. In Week 3 the market for funds is taken up. The Economist, 18 January 2024, reports Preqin data that more than four fifths of assets under management in infrastructure funds are allocated to Western markets, while the need is most pronounced in the global south; this is the pattern of Gardner and Henry in the previous section, and it needs checking against the Preqin source before it is quoted as a statistic. Weeks 5 and 6 take up the intermediary and the valuation problems.

SEMINAR TASKS

1. A pension fund tells you it wants inflation-linked long-duration cash flow. Identify which of the five claims it should test first, and how, using the four questions on the inflation slide.
2. If unlisted infrastructure valuations are appraisal-based, state the direction in which reported correlation with equities is biased, and explain why that matters for asset allocation.
3. Andonov and colleagues find a mismatch between the asset and the vehicle. Describe what a vehicle designed for the asset would look like, and explain why so few exist.

CLAIMS NOT VERIFIED, AND MATERIAL LEFT OFF THE SLIDES

The text below is carried over from the earlier draft of this section, which had fifteen slides, and has not been checked against sources, except where stated. It includes the cost overrun chart (Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl 2002, Journal of the American Planning Association 68(3), 279 to 295, 258 transport projects worth about US$90 billion), which is covered for China by the Ansar slides in the first section; the stylised chart of where infrastructure sits, which is not drawn from data; the table of infrastructure debt against equity, which sets up Week 3; and the J-curve. Other Economist readings kept for later weeks are listed in Resources/00 Economist readings - what to use where.md.

Block D
Infrastructure as an asset class
The claimed investment characteristics, and what the evidence does to them.
Indicative length 45 minutes

---

What it takes to be an asset class
An asset class is not a marketing category. It is a group of investments whose returns are driven by a common set of economic factors, which behave similarly under stress, and which are not spanned by existing asset classes already in the portfolio.

The last condition is the demanding one. If infrastructure returns can be reproduced by a combination of equities, bonds and real estate, then infrastructure is a strategy rather than an asset class, and it should be priced and benchmarked accordingly.
Weber ch. 2.1.

---

Five claims made for infrastructure as an investment
Stable cash flows
Essential services with inelastic demand, so revenue is less cyclical than corporate earnings.
Inflation linkage
Tariffs indexed by regulation or contract, so real returns are protected when inflation rises.
Low correlation
Returns driven by regulatory and contractual factors rather than by equity market sentiment.
Long duration
Cash flows extending decades, matching the liabilities of pension funds and life insurers.
Illiquidity premium
Compensation for accepting an asset that cannot be sold quickly, earned by investors who do not need to sell.
The common structure
Every claim is a claim about the contract or the regulatory settlement, not about the concrete. That is where to test them.

---

Inflation linkage is contractual, not physical
A regulated water network is protected against inflation because a regulatory formula indexes the allowed revenue, not because water is inherently inflation-proof. A contracted solar farm is protected for the life of its power purchase agreement and not one day longer. A merchant toll road is protected only to the extent that the concession permits toll increases and traffic tolerates them.

The practical question for any asset is therefore narrow and answerable: which index, applied to what share of revenue, with what lag, and until when.

---

The tail risk that recent data conceals
Start of the reconstructed US listed infrastructure return series used to test the low-risk claim.
Bianchi, Bornholt, Drew and Howard reconstruct US listed infrastructure index returns back to 1927 and analyse them in a Carhart four-factor framework. Low market beta and the value premium explain most of the return.

Their finding on risk is the one that matters for portfolio construction. Returns measured over recent decades understate long-run tail risk, which turns out to be comparable to that of a portfolio of US equities.

Some indices they examine are undesirable in a portfolio selection framework; others, notably broad and small utilities, do show diversification benefit. The asset class does not behave as one thing.
Bianchi, R. J., Bornholt, G., Drew, M. E. and Howard, M. F. (2014), Journal of Banking and Finance 42, 314–325.

---

The mismatch between the story and the vehicle
10 years
Typical contractual life of the closed-end private funds through which most institutions hold infrastructure.
Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh document what institutional investors say they want from infrastructure, which is long-term stable cash flow, and then what they actually buy, which is exposure through finite-horizon closed private funds.

The cash flows delivered by those funds display volatility and cyclicality similar to other private equity, and performance depends on quick deal exits in much the same way.

The asset may be a forty-year asset. The vehicle is a ten-year vehicle. Investors are exposed to the vehicle.
Andonov, A., Kräussl, R. and Rauh, J. (2021), The Review of Financial Studies 34(8), 3880–3934.

---

Listed and unlisted infrastructure
Listed
Daily prices, genuine liquidity, low minimum investment
Returns visibly correlated with equity markets, particularly in stress
Company-level exposure includes management, leverage and unrelated businesses
Reported volatility is real volatility
Unlisted
Appraisal-based valuations, typically quarterly
Reported volatility is smoothed by the appraisal process and understates the truth
Direct asset-level exposure, with control rights
Reported correlation with equities is partly an artefact of valuation method

---

Cost overrun by project type
Average cost overrun on 258 transport infrastructure projects, measured against the estimate made at the decision to build.
Flyvbjerg, B., Holm, M. S. and Buhl, S. (2002), Journal of the American Planning Association 68(3), 279–295. Sample of 258 transport projects worth about US$90 billion.

---

The illiquidity premium is an assumption, not a measurement
Investors are routinely told that unlisted infrastructure earns a premium for illiquidity. The premium is difficult to observe because the return series against which it would be measured is itself constructed from appraisals rather than transactions.

What can be said is narrower. Investors who do not need liquidity give up little by forgoing it, so illiquid assets are cheap for them relative to investors who do. Whether the market prices that difference as a systematic premium is contested, and the evidence in unlisted infrastructure is thin.

---

Infrastructure debt and infrastructure equity
Gatti ch. 8; Abor ch. 14 and ch. 15.

---

What survives the tests
The strong version of the asset class claim does not survive. Infrastructure returns are not uniformly stable, the recent record understates tail risk, and the vehicles through which the exposure is usually taken behave like private equity.

A weaker version does survive, and it is the version worth teaching. Certain infrastructure assets, held directly, with a regulated or contracted revenue base and a long holding period, do provide long-duration, partially indexed cash flow that is genuinely difficult to obtain elsewhere. The qualifications are doing real work in that sentence, and identifying which assets meet them is most of the job.

---

Where infrastructure is claimed to sit
The dispersion within infrastructure is wider than the distance between infrastructure and its neighbours.
Stylised illustration for teaching only. The figures are not estimates and are not drawn from a return series. The point of the exhibit is the ordering and its dependence on revenue model, not the magnitudes.

---

Correlation estimates deserve suspicion
The claim that infrastructure has low correlation with equities rests on return series that are, for unlisted assets, built from periodic appraisals. Appraisals are anchored on the previous appraisal and updated slowly, which smooths the series and mechanically reduces measured correlation and measured volatility.

The listed evidence, where prices are observed rather than estimated, shows correlation with equity markets that rises in stress, which is precisely when diversification is wanted. Whether the unlisted asset genuinely behaves differently or is merely measured differently is an open question, and it is the subject of Week 6.
Bianchi and others (2014); Andonov and others (2021).

---

The J-curve and why reported early performance misleads
A closed-end fund draws capital, pays fees, and invests before any asset has been improved or sold. Reported returns in the early years are therefore negative almost by construction, and reported returns in the later years benefit from the fees having already been paid.

For a course this matters in one specific way. Any comparison of infrastructure fund performance against a public market benchmark has to be made on the same basis, using a public market equivalent or an equivalent method, and comparisons made on internal rates of return alone are not meaningful.

---

Block D discussion
Seminar questions
A pension fund tells you it wants inflation-linked long-duration cash flow. Which of the five claims should it test first, and how?
If unlisted infrastructure valuations are appraisal-based, in what direction is reported correlation with equities biased, and why does that matter for asset allocation?
Andonov and colleagues find a mismatch between the asset and the vehicle. What would a vehicle designed for the asset actually look like, and why do so few exist?

title: Investors, Vehicles and Market Structure
notes:
OUTLINE OF THE SECTION (ABOUT 20 MINUTES, FIVE SLIDES)

The section asks who supplies the capital, through what vehicle, and at what price, and ends with a worked example of the fee on a fund. Slide 2 compares the routes into the asset and their costs, slide 3 is the interactive fee page, slide 4 sets out the direct alternative, and slide 5 summarises and says where each thread returns. The vehicle is a choice with consequences and not plumbing.

LIABILITIES DRIVE ALLOCATION (carried over from the earlier draft)

An investor allocates to infrastructure because of what it owes, not because of what infrastructure is. A mature defined benefit scheme paying inflation-linked pensions for forty years has a liability that regulated infrastructure matches unusually well. An insurer writing annuities has a similar problem and a different capital regime. An endowment with no fixed liabilities has no such need and buys infrastructure only if it expects a return premium. Read any allocation decision back to the liability and the apparent inconsistencies in market behaviour resolve. It also explains the geography of infrastructure investing, which follows the geography of funded pension systems.

THE BRITISH EXAMPLE

The Economist, 6 December 2022, Small pension funds are Britain's likeliest source of growth capital (Britain). It reports that defined benefit schemes held about £1.5 trillion and were £375 billion in surplus, that their holdings of British equities fell from a quarter of assets in 2008 to 2 per cent in 2021, and that with a surplus a scheme has no incentive to hold illiquid assets. Defined contribution schemes, with £500 billion in 2021 and set to reach £1 trillion by 2030, have the incentive to seek returns but a cap of 0.75 per cent a year on fund-management fees and daily dealing, which the article says does not suit illiquid assets. The Treasury and the Department for Work and Pensions were then considering raising the cap. The article is from 2022 and the rules may have changed, so check the current regime before quoting it. The funded-surplus figures are the article's, from sources I have not seen.

PUBLIC INVESTORS

Andonov, A., Kräussl, R. and Rauh, J. (2021), The Review of Financial Studies 34(8), 3880 to 3934: public investors hold funds with a 0.026 lower public market equivalent, a 1.810 percentage point lower net IRR and a 0.038 lower multiple than private investors (abstract and page 3884, Table 8 on page 3915). The abstract says ESG preferences and regulations explain 25 to 40 per cent of public investors' increased allocation to infrastructure and 30 per cent of their underperformance (page 3880). Note that this is a statement about the funds public investors choose, after controlling for fund characteristics, and not about all public investors' performance.

CONCENTRATION

The Economist, 18 January 2024, Why BlackRock is betting billions on infrastructure (Schumpeter): assets under management in infrastructure funds almost five-fold in a decade to US$1.3 trillion, and more than four fifths in Western markets, both attributed to Preqin, which I have not seen; the need for infrastructure is most pronounced in the global south. This is the pattern of the dual-hurdle test in the earlier section and the thesis of Week 3 stated in advance: capital is abundant, concentrated in a small number of very large investors, and unevenly matched to the assets that need it. It congregates in brownfield assets in stable jurisdictions with established regulatory regimes, where the least of the investment need lies. Repeat it in Week 3 and students will recognise it.

THE MAIN SUPPLIERS (from the earlier draft, Abor chs 14 to 16)

Pension funds: long-dated liabilities, constrained by governance capacity and size. Insurers: long liabilities and a capital regime that prices infrastructure debt favourably relative to equity. Sovereign wealth funds: no liabilities in the ordinary sense, long horizons and the scale to invest directly. Listed funds and corporates: assets held on balance sheet as strategic holdings. Development finance institutions: capital where commercial investors will not go, increasingly to mobilise others. Banks: still the dominant provider of construction-phase debt, with an appetite shaped by capital regulation. Ask which of these can hold a forty-year asset for forty years. The honest answer is sovereign wealth funds, a handful of very large pension plans and strategic corporates. Everyone else is a temporary owner.
