title: A Worked Example of Fee Drag
notes:
INTERACTIVE: web/fee-drag.html (button at top right)

The page is self-contained and open in a browser from Lecture Notes/Week 1/web/. The slide shows the default setting of the page; every slider in the page changes the figures, and the page has presets for the real asset returns and fee terms.

THE MODEL

One fund cycle, per 100 committed and drawn at the start. The fund's net asset value grows at the gross return less the management fee (taken from the fund's assets, charged either on commitments or on net asset value). At the end of the fund's life the fund sells at its net asset value less any discount, the whole-of-fund waterfall is applied (return of capital, then a preferred return at the hurdle compounded, then a catch-up if switched on, then the carried share), and the investor receives the rest and reinvests it in a new fund on the same terms. The direct route compounds at the gross return less an internal cost. The model was written twice, in Python (Lecture Notes/build/web_src/fee_model.py) and in JavaScript for the page (fee_model.js), and checked on 200 random settings; the two agree to better than one part in 10^13. The slide figure is drawn from the Python version.

RESULTS AT THE DEFAULT SETTING (8 per cent gross, 30 years, 1.5 per cent on commitments, 20 per cent carry over an 8 per cent hurdle with full catch-up, ten-year funds, direct cost 0.18 per cent)

Direct 7.82 per cent a year; funds 6.86 per cent; drag 114 basis points; 100 grows to 957 directly, 732 through funds and 1006 before any costs; 30 per cent of the gross profit is lost to the fund route. No carry is paid at 8 per cent gross, because the return after the fee is below the hurdle, so the whole drag is the management fee and its compounding. At the allowed returns the drag is similar: water at 7.2 per cent, 118 basis points (fund route 6.02 per cent against 7.02 direct); Ofgem's draft 7.64 per cent for electricity transmission, 116; gas at 8.04 per cent, 114. At 10 per cent gross the drag rises to 200 basis points because carry is now earned: the fund line on the right-hand chart is flat at 8 per cent between about 9 and 10.5 per cent gross, which is the manager's catch-up.

THE REAL FIGURES, AND WHERE THEY COME FROM

Asset returns: Independent Water Commission (2025), Final Report, page 323: Ofwat allowed 7.2 per cent on equity in nominal terms at Price Review 2024 and Ofgem's draft RIIO-3 cost of equity has midpoints of 7.64 per cent (electricity transmission) and 8.04 per cent (gas) including a 2 per cent inflation assumption; the Global Infrastructure Investor Association told the Commission that comparable regulated markets offer 8 to 12 per cent, a trade body's figure that the report attributes and does not endorse. Fee terms and fund life: see the notes to the previous slide, and Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021), page 3888, for a fund life of typically 10 to 12 years with extensions. Observed net returns: the same paper, Table 3, panel B, page 3897: mean net IRR 9.92 per cent and median 9.35 per cent for 210 infrastructure funds, and a public market equivalent of 0.93. The implied gross return is 12.5 per cent for the mean and 11.9 per cent for the median on the default terms. It is a calculation under the model's simplifications, and real funds draw capital over several years and use leverage, so it should not be read as a measurement. What it does show is that the observed net returns are not consistent with assets earning the allowed returns of regulated networks, so the funds must hold riskier assets or more leverage than the regulated yield in the sales pitch.

WHAT THE PAGE DOES NOT SHOW

The fund route can be worth its cost if it gives access to assets the investor could not otherwise reach or manage; the page measures the price and not the value. The direct route needs an internal team and the 0.18 per cent default is an all-asset average, so students should raise it. Real partnerships call fees on top of the commitment and measure the hurdle from each drawdown; the timing differs from the model's, but the size of the drag is of the same order. Step-downs in fees after the investment period are not modelled. Taxes are ignored.

TEACHING POINT

Do the arithmetic with the students on the page and not on a slide. It lands better as a calculation than as a claim, and it sets up Week 5. The conclusion is not that funds are indefensible, but that the fund route has to earn its cost through access. title: Summary
notes:

The module timetable (in the original Week 1 deck and the course outline) is: Week 3 private investment in infrastructure; Week 4 infrastructure financing and deal structuring; Week 5 intermediation and deal brokerage; Week 6 performance and valuation. SEMINAR TASKS

1. A mid-sized pension scheme cannot justify an internal infrastructure team. Identify the best available structure for it and state what that structure costs in return terms, using the fee page.
2. Explain why capital concentrates in brownfield assets in stable jurisdictions when the stated need is elsewhere.
3. State what would have to change for a ten-year fund to be an appropriate vehicle for a forty-year asset.

MATERIAL LEFT OFF THE SLIDES, AND CLAIMS NOT VERIFIED

The text below is carried over from the earlier draft of this section, which had eleven slides, and has not been checked against sources except where stated. It includes the development finance slide, which cites Hainz and Kleimeier (2012) and Broccolini and others (2021, World Bank Economic Review 35(2), 521 to 543) for the statement that multilateral lending crowds in roughly seven dollars of bank credit per dollar over three years; check that figure against the paper before quoting it, since the slide called it the empirical basis of blended finance. It also includes the consolidation slide, whose claims that a small number of managers raise the majority of capital and that several are divisions of private equity firms are not sourced here. The Economist article of 18 January 2024 supports part of this: General Atlantic, CVC and BlackRock bought infrastructure managers in 2023 and 2024, and BlackRock's US$12.5 billion purchase of Global Infrastructure Partners was reported by Reuters. Other Economist readings for Week 3 are in Resources/Week 3/Economist readings/ and are listed in Resources/00 Economist readings - what to use where.md.

Block E
Investors, vehicles and market structure
Who supplies the capital, through what structures, and why the structure shapes the outcome.
Indicative length 35 minutes

---

The main suppliers of capital
Pension funds
Long-dated, often inflation-linked liabilities. The natural holder in theory, constrained in practice by governance capacity and by size.
Insurers
Long liabilities and a regulatory capital regime that prices infrastructure debt favourably relative to equity.
Sovereign wealth funds
No liabilities in the ordinary sense, long horizons, and the scale to invest directly and take control positions.
Listed funds and corporates
Utilities, developers and conglomerates holding assets on balance sheet as strategic rather than portfolio investments.
Development finance institutions
Deploy capital where commercial investors will not, and increasingly to mobilise others rather than to lend alone.
Banks
Still the dominant provider of construction-phase debt, with an appetite shaped by capital regulation rather than by the asset.
Abor ch. 14, ch. 15 and ch. 16.

---

Liability structure drives allocation
An investor allocates to infrastructure because of what it owes, not because of what infrastructure is. A mature defined benefit pension scheme paying inflation-linked pensions for forty years has a liability that regulated infrastructure matches unusually well. An insurer writing annuities has a similar problem and a different capital regime. An endowment with no fixed liabilities has no such need and buys infrastructure only if it expects a return premium.

Read any allocation decision back to the liability and the apparent inconsistencies in market behaviour resolve.

---

Routes into the asset

---

The fund model and what it costs
The dominant vehicle is a closed-end limited partnership: a general partner raises capital from limited partners, invests it over an investment period, manages the assets, and returns capital through exits within a fixed life. The general partner charges a management fee on committed or invested capital and takes a share of profits above a hurdle.

The model is well suited to assets bought to be improved and sold. Its fit with assets bought to be held for forty years is poor, which is the structural point behind the Andonov finding in Block D. The fee load is the visible cost. The forced exit is the expensive one.
Andonov, Kräussl and Rauh (2021).

---

The direct investment model
Large Canadian and Australian plans built internal teams and buy assets directly, alone or in consortium.
The saving is not only the fee. Direct ownership removes the fund life, so the holding period can match the asset.
The cost is organisational: an internal team capable of underwriting and governing a regulated utility is expensive and hard to retain.
It is available only at scale. Below roughly the size at which an internal team can be justified, the fund route dominates.
Consortium ownership creates its own governance problem, which is why shareholders agreements matter as much as concession agreements. Week 4 returns to this.

---

Market structure in one paragraph
Capital for infrastructure is abundant, concentrated in a small number of very large investors, and unevenly matched to the assets that need it. It congregates in brownfield assets in stable jurisdictions with established regulatory regimes, which is where the least of the investment need lies. The parts of the market where new capacity is needed most, and where construction and political risk are highest, are served by development institutions, export credit agencies and a shrinking group of specialist banks.

That asymmetry, rather than any absolute shortage of capital, is the central problem of infrastructure finance.

---

A worked example of fee drag
Take an asset expected to deliver eight per cent a year over a thirty-year life. Held directly, the investor receives eight per cent less internal cost. Held through a fund charging one and a half per cent on invested capital and twenty per cent of profits above an eight per cent hurdle, and sold after ten years into a market that may or may not be receptive, the investor receives materially less and also loses the twenty years of holding that made the asset attractive in the first place.

The arithmetic is straightforward and worth doing on the board. The conclusion is not that funds are indefensible, but that the fund route has to earn its cost through access to assets the investor could not otherwise reach.

---

What development finance institutions actually do
Lend and invest where commercial capital will not, at pricing that reflects a development mandate rather than a required return.
Provide guarantees and credit enhancement that move a project across a rating threshold that commercial investors are bound by.
Absorb political risk that a private lender cannot diversify, which is the finding in Hainz and Kleimeier.
Mobilise rather than merely lend: Broccolini and colleagues estimate that multilateral lending crowds in roughly seven dollars of bank credit per dollar invested over three years.
Set environmental and social standards that then propagate through the syndicate, which is a form of regulation by lending.
Hainz and Kleimeier (2012); Broccolini and others (2021), World Bank Economic Review 35(2), 521–543.

---

Consolidation and its consequences
The manager side of the market has consolidated sharply. A small number of very large managers now raise the majority of capital committed to infrastructure, and several are divisions of firms whose primary business is private equity.

Two consequences follow. Fund sizes have grown faster than the supply of assets that meet the traditional definition, which is one force behind the boundary expansion in Block A. And the behavioural model of the buyer has shifted towards private equity practice, which is the mechanism behind the Andonov finding.

---

Block E discussion
Seminar questions
A mid-sized pension scheme cannot justify an internal infrastructure team. What is the best available structure for it, and what does that structure cost in return terms?
Why does capital concentrate in brownfield assets in stable jurisdictions when the stated need is elsewhere?
What would have to change for a ten-year fund to be an appropriate vehicle for a forty-year asset?

title: The Iron Law of Megaprojects
notes:
OUTLINE OF THE SECTION (ABOUT 20 MINUTES, FOUR SLIDES)

The section is the corrective to a week that otherwise reads like an investment prospectus, and it is placed last so that students leave with it. Two slides on the record (this one on overruns of cost and time, the next on forecasting), then two cases that show what the record looks like in practice and what good delivery does and does not mean: London 2012 and the Channel Tunnel. The sources are filed in Resources/Week 1/The Iron Law of Megaproject Management/.

SOURCES AND FIGURE

The figure is drawn from Table 4 of Flyvbjerg, B., Budzier, A. and Stewart, A. (2016), The Oxford Olympics Study 2016: cost and cost overrun at the Games, Saïd Business School Research Papers RP 2016-20 (SSRN 2804554), page 15. Average cost overrun in real terms, frequency of cost overrun and schedule overrun by type of large project: roads 20 per cent (9 of 10 projects), bridges and tunnels 34 (9 of 10), energy 36 (6 of 10), rail 45 (9 of 10), dams 90 (7 of 10), IT 107 (5 of 10), Olympics 156 (10 of 10); schedule overrun 38, 23, 38, 45, 44, 37 and 0 per cent. The table gives the average schedule length (3.3 to 8.2 years) and does not give the source of each row, so check the project types against the paper before quoting a single row.

The statement of the law is from Flyvbjerg, B. (2014), What you should know about megaprojects and why: an overview, Project Management Journal 45(2), 6 to 19; I used the author's draft (arXiv 1409.0003), so check page numbers against the published version. In the draft, page 9: nine out of ten megaprojects have cost overruns; overruns of up to 50 per cent in real terms are common and over 50 per cent not uncommon; overrun occurs in private as well as public projects; overruns have stayed high and constant for the 70-year period for which comparable data exist; and all countries and continents for which there are data suffer from overrun. Page 2: global megaproject spending is assessed at US$6 to 9 trillion annually, or 8 per cent of total global GDP. Page 10: preliminary Oxford results suggest that delays on dams are 45 per cent on average, so a dam planned to take ten years takes 14.5. The 'iron law' phrase is credited on page 30 to The Economist of 10 March 2012, which used it for transport infrastructure. The paper's Table 2 lists the cost overrun of 36 named projects, among them the Suez Canal (1,900 per cent), the Sydney Opera House (1,400), the Channel tunnel (80), Denver airport (200) and Boston's Big Dig (220); they are the examples to have ready when someone asks for names.

TEACHING POINT

Say the line and then give the number behind it at once. The formulation is memorable, and students repeat it without the evidence unless the evidence is supplied. Three points to draw out. First, the claim is not that projects sometimes go wrong but that overrun is the normal case. Second, the Olympics row shows the difference between schedule and cost: a fixed date removes schedule overrun (zero in the data) but not cost overrun (every Games with data). Third, the link back to the first section of Week 1: if nine in ten commitments are made on figures that turn out to be wrong, the aggregate misallocation is large enough to matter, which is the Ansar argument about debt and fragility. Success is rare enough in the data that, in Flyvbjerg's words, it can be studied only as small-sample research (draft page 11).

title: Forecasts Err in a Predictable Direction
notes:
SOURCES AND FIGURE

Flyvbjerg, B. (2009), Survival of the unfittest: why the worst infrastructure gets built, and what we can do about it, Oxford Review of Economic Policy 25(3), 344 to 367. I used the author's draft (arXiv 1303.6571), whose Tables 1 and 2 are on draft pages 25 and 26, so check the page numbers against the published article before quoting them. Table 1: cost overrun in constant prices, rail 58 projects, average 44.7 per cent, standard deviation 38.4; bridges and tunnels 33 projects, 33.8, standard deviation 62.4; roads 167 projects, 20.4, standard deviation 29.9; total 258 projects in 20 nations on five continents, from Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl (2002), Journal of the American Planning Association 68(3), 279 to 295. Table 2: inaccuracy of traffic forecasts, rail 25 projects, average minus 51.4 per cent, standard deviation 28.1; road 183 projects, plus 9.5 per cent, standard deviation 44.3, from Flyvbjerg, Holm and Buhl (2005), Journal of the American Planning Association 71(2), 131 to 146; the draft says 208 projects in 14 nations, and the earlier slide gave 210, so check the count against the 2005 paper. Rail passengers 51.4 per cent below estimate is, as the draft says, an average overestimate of 105.6 per cent, which is why the earlier version of this slide said 106. The signs are actual against forecast. For roads the average is small but the spread is wide: Flyvbjerg's 2014 overview says there is a fifty-fifty chance that demand is wrong by more than 20 per cent (page 9 of the draft).

Explanations. Technical error predicts errors centred on zero and improving over time; the draft says neither holds (the cost data show no improvement over the 70 years; page 3). Optimism bias predicts bias but not its persistence once it is known. Strategic misrepresentation predicts persistent, directional bias that survives better methods, which is what the data show. Probabilistic causation, the idea that overruns come from many small interacting factors in a complex delivery system, is the serious rival; the reference is to Love, Ahiaga-Dagbui and Irani (2016), Transportation Research Part A 92, 184 to 194, from the earlier draft, which I have not checked. Which explanation is right decides the remedy: better models fix error, reference class forecasting fixes bias, and only institutional checks fix misrepresentation.

Reference class forecasting. Draft page 12: the first use in practice was for the capital cost of the proposed Edinburgh tram line in 2004, where planners' estimate of £320 million was adjusted for optimism bias and the acceptable level of risk, giving £400 million with contingency at the 80 per cent level. The Oxford Olympics Study (page 4) quotes Kahneman (2011, page 251) calling the method the single most important piece of advice on increasing the accuracy of forecasting, and says it is used in the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Hong Kong, Denmark and Switzerland. The technique transfers to investment underwriting: an investor presented with a base case can ask for the distribution of outcomes for this class of asset. This is what Week 6 uses.

SURVIVAL OF THE UNFITTEST (left off the slide)

If the projects that get approved are those with the most optimistic numbers, the selection process rewards misrepresentation and not merit. The projects that look best on paper have the largest underestimates of cost and overestimates of benefit and so, other things equal, become the worst in reality (draft page 18 of the 2014 overview). Systematically inaccurate appraisal therefore does not only produce disappointing projects; it produces the wrong projects, because it corrupts the ranking on which selection depends. This is the idea to carry into Week 2, where public investment management exists to defend the ranking.

SOURCES AND FIGURES

Good delivery is possible, and the conditions under which it happened were specific. title: The Channel Tunnel: Asset against Investment
notes:
SOURCES AND FIGURE

Flyvbjerg, B. (2014), What you should know about megaprojects and why: an overview, Project Management Journal 45(2), 6 to 19; author's draft, arXiv 1409.0003, pages 9 and 10: the Channel tunnel, the longest underwater rail tunnel in Europe, had a cost overrun of 80 per cent in real terms (page 9); investors at the flotation were told that 10 per cent would be a reasonable allowance for unforeseen circumstances in construction costs; costs went 80 per cent over for construction and 140 per cent for financing, measured in real terms from the decision date; revenues have been half of those forecast; the internal rate of return is minus 14.5 per cent, with a total loss to the British economy of US$17.8 billion (page 10). The ex post evaluation behind this is Anguera, R. (2006), The Channel Tunnel: an ex post economic evaluation, Transportation Research Part A 40(4), 291 to 315, which concludes that the British economy would have been better off had the tunnel never been constructed (page 291). I have read the abstract of Anguera and not the paper. The same passage says each passenger is heavily subsidised by the private investors who lost their money when Eurotunnel went insolvent and was financially restructured, and draws the lesson that a megaproject may be a technological success and a financial failure. The page numbers refer to the draft and should be checked against the published article.

Left panel: Table 2 of the overview (draft page 29), the cost overrun in real terms of rail, tunnel and bridge projects: Humber bridge 180 per cent, Copenhagen metro 150, Boston to New York to Washington railway 130, Great Belt rail tunnel 120, Shinkansen Joetsu line 100, Channel tunnel 80, London Jubilee Line extension 80, High-speed Rail Line South in the Netherlands 60, Great Belt east bridge 50. The table is a list of examples chosen to illustrate the point and is not a random sample. The Great Belt rail tunnel is described on page 10 as non-viable, along with Sydney's Lane Cove tunnel, the airport rail links at Stockholm and Oslo, and the Copenhagen metro; the earlier draft (Flyvbjerg 2009, page 4) says that it could be paid for only by cross-subsidy from the revenues of a nearby motorway bridge.

Right panel: the three numbers are those quoted above, with revenue drawn at minus 50 per cent from 'revenues have been half of those forecast'. The construction overrun of 80 per cent is measured from the decision date; other studies measure it differently (a 2008 table I saw in a search shows 69 per cent for Eurotunnel, and a trade report shows construction costs roughly doubling), so quote 80 per cent only with the source.

Not verified: the details of Eurotunnel's restructuring. A search of the company's reports shows that the Paris Commercial Court opened a safeguard procedure on 2 August 2006 and approved a plan on 15 January 2007, and that debt was reported as about £6.2 billion before the plan and £2.8 billion after it, with shareholders largely diluted. I could not open the company documents, so these are secondary.

TEACHING POINT

The distinction between a successful asset and a successful investment is the whole lesson. Passengers use a fast, convenient and competitive service every day, and the people who financed it lost their money. The cost overrun alone does not explain this, since 80 per cent is in the middle of the list; the failures were of financing cost, which was 140 per cent over, and of revenue, which was half. That ties to Week 4 (risk allocation and the capital structure) and to Week 6 (cover ratios calculated on an optimistic base case).

Block F
The iron law of megaproject management
What the delivery record shows, and why it belongs in the first week.
Indicative length 40 minutes

---

The iron law
Over budget, over time, over and over again.
Flyvbjerg, B. (2014), Project Management Journal 45(2), 6–19.
Flyvbjerg, B. (ed.) (2017), The Oxford Handbook of Megaproject Management, ch. 1.

---

How often projects run over
Nine in ten
Share of megaprojects in Flyvbjerg’s samples that exceed their approved budget.
The claim is not that projects sometimes go wrong. It is that overrun is the normal case, that it has not improved over the several decades for which records exist, and that it holds across countries, sectors and procurement routes.

Flyvbjerg puts global megaproject spending at six to nine trillion dollars a year, or roughly eight per cent of world output. If nine in ten of those commitments are made on numbers that turn out to be wrong, the aggregate misallocation is large enough to matter macroeconomically.

That is the connection back to Block B, and to the Ansar argument about debt and fragility.
Flyvbjerg (2014).

---

Demand forecasts are wrong in a predictable direction
Rail passenger forecasts are overestimated by an average of 106 per cent, and half of road projects miss forecast traffic by more than twenty per cent.
Flyvbjerg, B., Skamris Holm, M. K. and Buhl, S. L. (2005), Journal of the American Planning Association 71(2), 131–146. Sample of 210 projects in 14 nations. Rail figure is the average overestimate of passengers; road figure is the share of projects where actual traffic differs from forecast by more than twenty per cent in either direction.

---

Four explanations, and what each implies
Technical error. Forecasting is hard and the models are imperfect. This would predict errors centred on zero and improving over time. Neither holds.
Optimism bias. Planners are systematically over-optimistic, a psychological regularity documented well beyond infrastructure. This predicts bias but not its persistence once known.
Strategic misrepresentation. Promoters understate costs and overstate demand because that is how projects get approved. This predicts persistent, directional bias that survives better methods, which is what the data show.
Probabilistic causation. Overruns arise from the interaction of many small factors in a complex delivery system rather than from deception. This is the principal challenge to the Flyvbjerg account.
Which explanation is right determines the remedy. Better models fix error. Reference class forecasting fixes bias. Only institutional checks fix misrepresentation.
Flyvbjerg (2002); Love, P. E. D., Ahiaga-Dagbui, D. D. and Irani, Z. (2016), Transportation Research Part A 92, 184–194.

---

Reference class forecasting
245 dams
Sample used to establish the outside view for large hydropower projects.
Ansar and colleagues take an outside view: rather than modelling a project from its own components, compare it with the distribution of outcomes for the class of projects it belongs to.

On their sample, actual costs of large dams exceeded estimated costs by a large margin on average, and schedule overruns were routine. The method is now embedded in United Kingdom appraisal guidance in the form of optimism bias uplifts.

The technique transfers directly to investment underwriting. An investor presented with a base case can ask what the distribution of outcomes for this class of asset has been, and adjust accordingly.
Ansar, A., Flyvbjerg, B., Budzier, A. and Lunn, D. (2014), Energy Policy 69, 43–56. Headline overrun figures to be confirmed against the published paper before delivery.

---

Survival of the unfittest
If the projects that get approved are those with the most optimistic numbers, then the selection process rewards misrepresentation rather than merit. The project that should have been built loses to the project whose promoters were most willing to understate its cost.

The implication is uncomfortable and worth stating plainly. Systematically inaccurate appraisal does not merely produce disappointing projects. It produces the wrong projects, because it corrupts the ranking on which selection depends.
Flyvbjerg (2014); Flyvbjerg (ed.) (2017), ch. 1.

---

Why this belongs in Week 1
What it changes about the rest of the module
A financial model is only as good as the cost and revenue forecasts underneath it, which we now know are biased
Cover ratios calculated on a base case inherit the base case’s optimism, which is the Week 6 problem
Risk allocation in Week 4 is the contractual response to exactly these failures
Appraisal and gateway institutions in Week 2 are the public response
What it should not become
A counsel of despair. Some projects are delivered well and the block should name a few
A claim that the private sector is immune. The same biases appear in privately promoted schemes
A reason to avoid infrastructure. The evidence argues for better selection, not for less investment
A single explanation. Love and colleagues offer a serious alternative and Week 6 gives it a hearing

---

The four sublimes
Political
The satisfaction of building monuments. Projects are visible, attributable and durable in a way that current spending is not.
Technological
The engineering appeal of the longest, tallest, fastest. The professionals who design projects want to design ambitious ones.
Economic
The business and employment created by construction, which accrues to identifiable firms and unions regardless of whether the asset is used.
Aesthetic
The pleasure of an iconic object. Bilbao and Sydney are cited in support of schemes with no comparable prospect.
What they have in common
Each supplies a constituency with an interest in the project proceeding, and none of them is an interest in the project being accurately costed.
Flyvbjerg (2014); Flyvbjerg (ed.) (2017), ch. 1.

---

Two cases worth keeping
The Channel Tunnel
Delivered, and a genuine engineering achievement
Construction costs ran far above the estimate on which investors subscribed
Traffic fell well short of forecast for many years after opening
Original equity was effectively destroyed while the asset itself continued to operate
The distinction between a successful asset and a successful investment is the whole lesson
London 2012
Delivered on time and within the revised budget, which is rare enough to be studied
Systems integration was treated as a discipline in its own right rather than as project administration
A separate delivery authority was created with a clear remit and a fixed deadline
The immovable deadline was itself a governance device
Flyvbjerg ch. 21 sets out the mechanism in detail
Flyvbjerg (ed.) (2017), ch. 21. Channel Tunnel figures to be confirmed before delivery.

---

The distinction that matters for an investor
A project can be a triumph of engineering and a disaster for the people who financed it. The Channel Tunnel operates, carries millions of passengers, and did what its promoters said it would do physically. It also wiped out the investors who paid for it.

For this module the implication is precise. The question is never whether the asset will work. It is whether the cash flows will arrive in the amounts and at the times assumed, and who bears the loss if they do not. That question is the subject of Weeks 4, 5 and 6.

The Global Infrastructure Advisory Panel
The panel is a standing group of practitioners drawn from the Department’s Global Land Economy network. Members deliver sessions, supply the live questions on which group projects are based, advise on case selection, and act as assessors for the Week 8 presentations.

---

Group project: what a good answer looks like
A recommendation
Not a survey of considerations. State what should be done, then defend it against the strongest objection.
A number
Every recommendation has a financial consequence. Quantify it, state the assumptions, and show what would change the answer.
A risk allocation
Name who bears each material risk under your proposal and why that party is the efficient bearer of it.
An honest range
Give the base case and the distribution around it. A single point estimate presented without a range will be marked down.
A stakeholder map
Identify who must agree, what each party needs, and where your proposal is politically vulnerable.
Brevity
A report that cannot state its recommendation in the first paragraph has not finished thinking.

---

Why the module brings three programmes together
The Department teaches three taught MPhils, and they currently meet in one place: Research Methods, which is a methods module rather than a subject. Infrastructure is the natural subject for that meeting, because a large project cannot be understood from any single position.

Someone who can price a project usually cannot get it consented. Someone who can get it consented usually cannot fund it. Someone who can assess its emissions and the policy instruments acting on it is rarely asked what a debt service cover ratio is. Every week of this module names the modules it draws on, grouped by programme, and the group project teams are composed across programmes on purpose.

---

What each programme brings, and what will be unfamiliar
Real Estate Finance
Brings pricing, capital structure, discounted cash flow, valuation under uncertainty, and the vocabulary of the capital markets.

Will find it unfamiliar that a project has to be consented before it can be financed, and that the regulatory settlement is renegotiated rather than fixed.
Planning, Growth and Regeneration
Brings the consenting process, who objects and on what grounds, how land value is captured, and how a public programme is evaluated after the fact.

Will find the capital stack and the cover ratio unfamiliar, and may be surprised that a lender’s veto over a scheme is in practice stronger than a planner’s.
Environmental Policy
Brings instrument choice, the economics of externalities, the energy system, and the law the transition actually runs on.

Will find it unfamiliar how a project is financed in detail, and what a commitment about future emissions is worth to a credit committee.

---

Team formation
Teams of four to five, formed in this session, and composed across programmes. Aim for at least two of the three MPhils in every team, and all three where the numbers allow.
A team drawn from a single programme will produce a report with a predictable blind spot, and it will be visible to the panel in Week 8.
Mix quantitative capability deliberately as well. A team with nobody comfortable in a spreadsheet will struggle in Week 6.
Each team nominates a coordinator, whose job is scheduling and submission rather than authorship.
Project questions are allocated in Week 2 once the panel has confirmed the live issues for this year.
Teams that cannot resolve an internal problem should raise it early. A dispute reported in Week 7 cannot be fixed.

Supervisions and how to use them
Supervisions accompany the lectures and are where the individual coursework is discussed.
Come with a specific difficulty rather than a general one. A supervision spent explaining what a cover ratio is has been wasted; one spent arguing about which ratio the lender should care about has not.
The two formative exercises are set in Week 3 and Week 6 and discussed in the supervision that follows each.
Reading is set per week in the module reading list. Two articles a week are required; the remainder support the group project.

Use of generative tools
The Department’s policy applies in full and students should read it. For this module two practical points are worth stating in the first session. Any figure, citation or quotation that appears in submitted work is the student’s responsibility to verify, whatever produced it, and fabricated citations are treated as an academic offence rather than as a technical error.

The second point is about learning rather than conduct. The judgement this module assesses, which is what to recommend under uncertainty and what to do when the numbers are contested, is precisely the part that cannot be delegated.

Infrastructure is not one thing, and the properties that matter are contractual rather than physical.
